questiontext.text:
Match the thermodynamic systems/walls with their corresponding examples or characteristics:

Column IColumn II
1. Open systemP. Reactants in a thermos flask
2. Closed systemQ. Boundary that prevents heat transfer
3. Isolated systemR. Reactants in an open beaker
4. Adiabatic wallS. Reactants in a closed conducting steel vessel

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thermodynamic systems are classified according to whether matter and energy can cross the boundary between the system and its surroundings.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
An open system allows exchange of both matter and energy with the surroundings, as seen for reactants in an open beaker. A closed system prevents matter exchange but allows energy exchange, as in a closed vessel made of a conducting material like steel or copper. An isolated system permits neither matter nor energy exchange, as in a thermos flask. An adiabatic wall is a thermally insulated boundary that does not allow heat transfer between the system and surroundings.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matching pairs are: Open system with reactants in an open beaker; Closed system with reactants in a closed conducting steel vessel; Isolated system with reactants in a thermos flask; and Adiabatic wall with a boundary that prevents heat transfer.

questiontext.text:
Match the thermodynamic concepts with their correct definitions:

Column IColumn II
1. State functionP. Property independent of the quantity of matter
2. Extensive propertyQ. Process with no heat transfer across the boundary
3. Intensive propertyR. Quantity whose value depends only on the state of the system
4. Adiabatic processS. Property whose value depends on the quantity of matter

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thermodynamic variables and processes are defined by their path dependence, scaling with system size, and boundary constraints.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
A state function (such as \(p\), \(V\), \(T\), \(U\), or \(H\)) depends only on the initial and final states of the system and not on how the state is reached. An extensive property (such as mass, volume, or enthalpy) depends on the quantity or size of matter present. An intensive property (such as temperature, density, or pressure) is independent of the quantity of matter present. An adiabatic process is one in which no heat is transferred between the system and the surroundings (\(q = 0\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, State function pairs with a quantity depending only on the state of the system; Extensive property pairs with a property depending on the quantity of matter; Intensive property pairs with a property independent of the quantity of matter; and Adiabatic process pairs with a process having no heat transfer across the boundary.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q03 - IUPAC sign conventions for heat and work

questiontext.text:
Match each energy transfer process with its correct IUPAC sign convention in chemical thermodynamics:

Column IColumn II
1. Heat transferred from surroundings to systemP. \(w < 0\)
2. Heat transferred from system to surroundingsQ. \(q > 0\)
3. Work done on the systemR. \(q < 0\)
4. Work done by the systemS. \(w > 0\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to IUPAC conventions in chemical thermodynamics, any energy transferred into the system increases its internal energy and is assigned a positive sign, while any energy leaving the system decreases its internal energy and is assigned a negative sign.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
When heat is transferred from the surroundings to the system, the internal energy increases, so \(q > 0\). When heat is transferred from the system to the surroundings, the internal energy decreases, so \(q < 0\). When work is done on the system (such as compression), the internal energy increases, so \(w > 0\). When work is done by the system (such as expansion), the internal energy decreases, so \(w < 0\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, heat transferred from surroundings to system corresponds to \(q > 0\); heat transferred from system to surroundings corresponds to \(q < 0\); work done on the system corresponds to \(w > 0\); and work done by the system corresponds to \(w < 0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q04 - First law expressions for special processes

questiontext.text:
Match each thermodynamic process for an ideal gas with its corresponding mathematical expression:

Column IColumn II
1. Isothermal reversible expansionP. \(\Delta U = w_{\mathrm{ad}}\)
2. Isothermal free expansion into vacuumQ. \(\Delta U = q_v\)
3. Process at constant volumeR. \(w = -2.303\,nRT\log\frac{V_f}{V_i}\)
4. Adiabatic processS. \(w = 0,\; \Delta U = 0\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Applying the first law of thermodynamics \(\Delta U = q + w\) with \(w = -\int p_{\mathrm{ex}}\,dV\) under specific boundary conditions yields distinct simplified relations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
For an isothermal reversible expansion of \(n\text{ mol}\) of an ideal gas, \(p_{\mathrm{ex}} \approx p = \frac{nRT}{V}\), so \(w = -2.303\,nRT\log\frac{V_f}{V_i}\). For an isothermal free expansion into a vacuum, \(p_{\mathrm{ex}} = 0\) gives \(w = 0\), and experimentally \(q = 0\), so \(\Delta U = 0\). At constant volume, \(\Delta V = 0\) makes \(w = 0\), so \(\Delta U = q_v\). In an adiabatic process, \(q = 0\), so \(\Delta U = w_{\mathrm{ad}}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, isothermal reversible expansion matches \(w = -2.303\,nRT\log\frac{V_f}{V_i}\); isothermal free expansion into vacuum matches \(w = 0, \Delta U = 0\); constant volume process matches \(\Delta U = q_v\); and adiabatic process matches \(\Delta U = w_{\mathrm{ad}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q05 - Standard enthalpy changes and phase or atomisation processes

questiontext.text:
Match the standard enthalpy symbols with the corresponding chemical or physical processes:

Column IColumn II
1. \(\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H^\ominus\)P. \(\mathrm{CO_2(s) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\)
2. \(\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}}H^\ominus\)Q. \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)}\)
3. \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sub}}H^\ominus\)R. \(\mathrm{H_2O(s) \rightarrow H_2O(l)}\)
4. \(\Delta_a H^\ominus\)S. \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each standard enthalpy symbol denotes the enthalpy change for \(1\text{ mol}\) of a substance undergoing a specific phase transformation or bond-breaking process under standard pressure (\(1\text{ bar}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H^\ominus\) is the standard enthalpy of fusion (melting of solid to liquid), corresponding to \(\mathrm{H_2O(s) \rightarrow H_2O(l)}\). \(\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}}H^\ominus\) is the standard enthalpy of vaporisation (liquid to gas), corresponding to \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\). \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sub}}H^\ominus\) is the standard enthalpy of sublimation (direct conversion of solid to vapour), corresponding to \(\mathrm{CO_2(s) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\). \(\Delta_a H^\ominus\) is the enthalpy of atomisation (breaking all bonds to form gaseous atoms), corresponding to \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, \(\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H^\ominus\) pairs with \(\mathrm{H_2O(s) \rightarrow H_2O(l)}\); \(\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}}H^\ominus\) pairs with \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\); \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sub}}H^\ominus\) pairs with \(\mathrm{CO_2(s) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\); and \(\Delta_a H^\ominus\) pairs with \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q06 - Change in gaseous moles for chemical reactions

questiontext.text:
Match each balanced chemical reaction with its value of \(\Delta n_g\) used in \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\):

Column IColumn II
1. \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\)P. \(\Delta n_g = -2\)
2. \(\mathrm{C(graphite, s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\)Q. \(\Delta n_g = -1\)
3. \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightarrow 2NH_3(g)}\)R. \(\Delta n_g = 0\)
4. \(\mathrm{2A(g) + B(g) \rightarrow 2D(g)}\)S. \(\Delta n_g = +1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four balanced chemical/physical equations are given with specified physical states (solid, liquid, gas).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Only gaseous reactants and products contribute to \(\Delta n_g\); solids and liquids are excluded.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Delta n_g = (\text{total moles of gaseous products}) - (\text{total moles of gaseous reactants})\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\): \(\Delta n_g = 1 - 0 = +1\).
2. For \(\mathrm{C(graphite, s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\): \(\Delta n_g = 1 - 1 = 0\).
3. For \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightarrow 2NH_3(g)}\): \(\Delta n_g = 2 - (1 + 3) = -2\).
4. For \(\mathrm{2A(g) + B(g) \rightarrow 2D(g)}\): \(\Delta n_g = 2 - (2 + 1) = -1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying each stoichiometric difference confirms: \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\) has \(\Delta n_g = +1\); \(\mathrm{C(graphite) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)}\) has \(\Delta n_g = 0\); \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightarrow 2NH_3(g)}\) has \(\Delta n_g = -2\); and \(\mathrm{2A(g) + B(g) \rightarrow 2D(g)}\) has \(\Delta n_g = -1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q07 - Standard molar enthalpies of formation at 298 K

questiontext.text:
Match each substance with its standard molar enthalpy of formation \(\Delta_f H^\ominus\) at \(298\text{ K}\):

Column IColumn II
1. \(\mathrm{C(graphite)}\)P. \(-285.83\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
2. \(\mathrm{C(diamond)}\)Q. \(0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
3. \(\mathrm{CO_2(g)}\)R. \(+1.89\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
4. \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)S. \(-393.51\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
By convention, the standard molar enthalpy of formation \(\Delta_f H^\ominus\) of an element in its reference state (most stable state of aggregation at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(1\text{ bar}\)) is zero.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
For carbon, graphite is the reference state, so \(\Delta_f H^\ominus[\mathrm{C(graphite)}] = 0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), whereas diamond is a less stable allotrope with \(\Delta_f H^\ominus[\mathrm{C(diamond)}] = +1.89\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). From standard thermodynamic data at \(298\text{ K}\), \(\Delta_f H^\ominus[\mathrm{CO_2(g)}] = -393.51\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta_f H^\ominus[\mathrm{H_2O(l)}] = -285.83\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{C(graphite)}\) pairs with \(0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); \(\mathrm{C(diamond)}\) pairs with \(+1.89\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); \(\mathrm{CO_2(g)}\) pairs with \(-393.51\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); and \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) pairs with \(-285.83\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q08 - Laws of thermodynamics and Hess law statements

questiontext.text:
Match each thermodynamic law with its characteristic statement:

Column IColumn II
1. First law of thermodynamicsP. Entropy of a pure crystalline substance approaches zero at \(0\text{ K}\)
2. Second law of thermodynamicsQ. Standard reaction enthalpy is the sum of enthalpies of intermediate steps
3. Third law of thermodynamicsR. Energy of an isolated system is constant
4. Hess's lawS. Total entropy increases in a spontaneous process

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The laws of thermodynamics govern energy conservation, spontaneity direction, absolute entropy at absolute zero, and path independence of enthalpy changes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
The first law of thermodynamics states that the energy of an isolated system is constant (\(\Delta U = q + w\)). The second law of thermodynamics establishes that for a spontaneous process, the total entropy of system and surroundings increases (\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{total}} > 0\)). The third law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of any pure crystalline substance approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero (\(0\text{ K}\)). Hess's law states that if a reaction occurs in several steps, its standard reaction enthalpy is the sum of the standard enthalpies of the intermediate reactions at the same temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the first law matches constancy of energy in an isolated system; the second law matches increase in total entropy for a spontaneous process; the third law matches zero entropy of a pure crystal at \(0\text{ K}\); and Hess's law matches summation of intermediate reaction enthalpies.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q09 - Entropy changes in physical and chemical processes

questiontext.text:
Match each process with the correct explanation for its entropy change \(\Delta S\):

Column IColumn II
1. A liquid crystallises into a solidP. \(\Delta S > 0\); particles oscillate more vigorously in the lattice
2. Temperature of a crystalline solid is raised from \(0\text{ K}\) to \(115\text{ K}\)Q. \(\Delta S < 0\); molecules attain a more ordered state
3. \(2\mathrm{NaHCO_3(s) \rightarrow Na_2CO_3(s) + CO_2(g) + H_2O(g)}\)R. \(\Delta S > 0\); one molecule dissociates into two gaseous atoms
4. \(\mathrm{H_2(g) \rightarrow 2H(g)}\)S. \(\Delta S > 0\); solid reactant forms two gaseous products

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Entropy \(S\) is a measure of randomness or disorder. Transitions to more ordered states decrease entropy (\(\Delta S < 0\)), whereas increasing temperature, increasing the number of particles, or forming gaseous products increases entropy (\(\Delta S > 0\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
When a liquid crystallises into a solid, molecules become arranged in an ordered lattice, so \(\Delta S < 0\). Raising the temperature of a crystalline solid from \(0\text{ K}\) to \(115\text{ K}\) increases thermal agitation and oscillation about lattice positions, so \(\Delta S > 0\). Decomposition of solid \(\mathrm{NaHCO_3}\) produces gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), greatly increasing disorder (\(\Delta S > 0\)). Dissociation of \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) into \(2\mathrm{H(g)}\) increases the number of gaseous particles, increasing disorder (\(\Delta S > 0\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, liquid crystallisation matches \(\Delta S < 0\) due to ordering; heating a crystal from \(0\text{ K}\) to \(115\text{ K}\) matches \(\Delta S > 0\) due to lattice oscillations; decomposition of \(\mathrm{NaHCO_3(s)}\) matches \(\Delta S > 0\) due to gaseous product formation; and \(\mathrm{H_2(g) \rightarrow 2H(g)}\) matches \(\Delta S > 0\) due to dissociation into two gaseous atoms.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q10 - Key thermodynamic equations and their physical meaning

questiontext.text:
Match each thermodynamic equation with what it defines or relates:

Column IColumn II
1. \(H = U + pV\)P. Entropy change for a reversible process
2. \(C_p - C_v = R\)Q. Definition of Gibbs function
3. \(G = H - TS\)R. Definition of enthalpy
4. \(\Delta S = \frac{q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}\)S. Relation between molar heat capacities for an ideal gas

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thermodynamic state functions and heat capacities are linked by fundamental defining equations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
\(H = U + pV\) is the definition of enthalpy \(H\). \(C_p - C_v = R\) relates the molar heat capacities at constant pressure and constant volume for \(1\text{ mol}\) of an ideal gas. \(G = H - TS\) defines the Gibbs energy or Gibbs function \(G\). \(\Delta S = \frac{q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}\) gives the entropy change for a reversible process at temperature \(T\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, \(H = U + pV\) matches the definition of enthalpy; \(C_p - C_v = R\) matches the ideal gas heat capacity relation; \(G = H - TS\) matches the definition of Gibbs function; and \(\Delta S = \frac{q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}\) matches the reversible entropy change.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q11 - Born-Haber cycle steps for sodium chloride

questiontext.text:
Match each step in the Born-Haber cycle of \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) with its corresponding enthalpy term:

Column IColumn II
1. \(\mathrm{Na(s) \rightarrow Na(g)}\)P. Electron gain enthalpy, \(\Delta_{\mathrm{eg}}H^\ominus\)
2. \(\mathrm{Na(g) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + e^-}\)Q. Lattice enthalpy, \(\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus\)
3. \(\mathrm{Cl(g) + e^- \rightarrow Cl^-(g)}\)R. Sublimation enthalpy, \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sub}}H^\ominus\)
4. \(\mathrm{Na^+Cl^-(s) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g)}\)S. Ionization enthalpy, \(\Delta_i H^\ominus\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A Born-Haber cycle breaks down the formation or dissociation of an ionic crystal into a sequence of thermochemical steps involving sublimation, bond dissociation, ionization, electron gain, and lattice dissociation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
\(\mathrm{Na(s) \rightarrow Na(g)}\) is the sublimation of solid sodium metal (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{sub}}H^\ominus\)). \(\mathrm{Na(g) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + e^-}\) is the ionization of gaseous sodium atoms (\(\Delta_i H^\ominus\)). \(\mathrm{Cl(g) + e^- \rightarrow Cl^-(g)}\) is the electron gain by gaseous chlorine atoms (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{eg}}H^\ominus\)). \(\mathrm{Na^+Cl^-(s) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g)}\) is the dissociation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of solid ionic compound into gaseous ions, which defines lattice enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{Na(s) \rightarrow Na(g)}\) matches sublimation enthalpy; \(\mathrm{Na(g) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + e^-}\) matches ionization enthalpy; \(\mathrm{Cl(g) + e^- \rightarrow Cl^-(g)}\) matches electron gain enthalpy; and \(\mathrm{Na^+Cl^-(s) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g)}\) matches lattice enthalpy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q12 - Effect of temperature on spontaneity from enthalpy and entropy signs

questiontext.text:
Match the sign combinations of \(\Delta_r H^\ominus\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus\) with the spontaneity behaviour of the reaction:

Column IColumn II
1. \(\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0,\; \Delta_r S^\ominus > 0\)P. Non-spontaneous at low \(T\), spontaneous at high \(T\)
2. \(\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0,\; \Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\)Q. Non-spontaneous at all temperatures
3. \(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0,\; \Delta_r S^\ominus > 0\)R. Spontaneous at all temperatures
4. \(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0,\; \Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\)S. Spontaneous at low \(T\), non-spontaneous at high \(T\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At constant temperature and pressure, spontaneity is governed by the Gibbs equation \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = \Delta_r H^\ominus - T\Delta_r S^\ominus\), where \(\Delta_r G^\ominus < 0\) indicates a spontaneous process.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. When \(\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus > 0\), both \(\Delta_r H^\ominus\) and \(-T\Delta_r S^\ominus\) are negative, so \(\Delta_r G^\ominus < 0\) at all temperatures (always spontaneous).
2. When \(\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\), \(-T\Delta_r S^\ominus\) is positive; thus \(\Delta_r G^\ominus < 0\) only at low temperatures where \(|\Delta_r H^\ominus| > |T\Delta_r S^\ominus|\), and becomes positive at high temperatures.
3. When \(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus > 0\), \(-T\Delta_r S^\ominus\) is negative; thus \(\Delta_r G^\ominus > 0\) at low temperatures and becomes negative at high temperatures where \(T\Delta_r S^\ominus > \Delta_r H^\ominus\).
4. When \(\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0\) and \(\Delta_r S^\ominus < 0\), both \(\Delta_r H^\ominus\) and \(-T\Delta_r S^\ominus\) are positive, so \(\Delta_r G^\ominus > 0\) at all temperatures (always non-spontaneous).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \((\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0, \Delta_r S^\ominus > 0)\) is spontaneous at all temperatures; \((\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0, \Delta_r S^\ominus < 0)\) is spontaneous at low \(T\) and non-spontaneous at high \(T\); \((\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0, \Delta_r S^\ominus > 0)\) is non-spontaneous at low \(T\) and spontaneous at high \(T\); and \((\Delta_r H^\ominus > 0, \Delta_r S^\ominus < 0)\) is non-spontaneous at all temperatures.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q13 - Numerical values of internal energy and enthalpy changes

questiontext.text:
Match each process with its calculated value of \(\Delta U\), \(\Delta H\), or \(\Delta_f H^\ominus\):

Column IColumn II
1. \(701\text{ J}\) heat absorbed by system and \(394\text{ J}\) work done by systemP. \(-46.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
2. Vaporisation of \(1\text{ mol}\) \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) at \(373\text{ K}\) (\(\Delta H = 41.00\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(R = 8.3\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\))Q. \(+307\text{ J}\)
3. \(\Delta_f H^\ominus(\mathrm{NH_3, g})\) given \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightarrow 2NH_3(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^\ominus = -92.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)R. \(-13.56\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
4. Converting \(1\text{ mol}\) \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) at \(100^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to ice at \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\) (\(c = 4.2\text{ J g}^{-1\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H = 6.00\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\))S. \(+37.904\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four numerical processes from chemical thermodynamics are provided with heat, work, enthalpy, heat capacity, and temperature data.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
By IUPAC convention, heat absorbed is positive (\(q > 0\)), work done by the system is negative (\(w < 0\)), and cooling/freezing releases heat (\(\Delta H < 0\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. \(\Delta U = q + w\)
2. \(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT\)
3. \(\Delta_f H^\ominus = \frac{1}{2}\Delta_r H^\ominus\) for forming \(2\text{ mol}\) product
4. \(\Delta H = -mc\Delta T - \Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(\Delta U = +701\text{ J} + (-394\text{ J}) = +307\text{ J}\).
2. For \(\mathrm{H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(g)}\), \(\Delta n_g = 1\), so \(\Delta U = 41.00\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} - (1)(8.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1})(373\text{ K}) = 41.00 - 3.096 = +37.904\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
3. Since \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NH_3(g)}\) are formed, \(\Delta_f H^\ominus(\mathrm{NH_3}) = \frac{-92.4}{2} = -46.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
4. Cooling \(18\text{ g}\) water by \(100^\circ\mathrm{C}\): \(\Delta H_1 = -18 \times 4.2 \times 100 = -7560\text{ J mol}^{-1} = -7.56\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Freezing: \(\Delta H_2 = -6.00\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Total \(\Delta H = -7.56 - 6.00 = -13.56\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All units and signs are consistent: the first process gives \(+307\text{ J}\), the second gives \(+37.904\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), the third gives \(-46.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), and the fourth gives \(-13.56\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q14 - Gibbs energy criteria and equilibrium constant

questiontext.text:
Match each Gibbs energy condition with its corresponding equilibrium consequence:

Column IColumn II
1. \(\Delta_r G^\ominus < 0\)P. \(K = 1\)
2. \(\Delta_r G^\ominus > 0\)Q. System is at dynamic equilibrium
3. \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = 0\)R. \(K > 1\) (products favoured at equilibrium)
4. \(\Delta_r G = 0\)S. \(K < 1\) (reactants favoured at equilibrium)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard Gibbs energy change \(\Delta_r G^\ominus\) is related to the equilibrium constant \(K\) by \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = -RT\ln K\), while the actual reaction Gibbs energy \(\Delta_r G\) determines whether a system is at equilibrium.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. When \(\Delta_r G^\ominus < 0\), \(-RT\ln K < 0 \implies \ln K > 0 \implies K > 1\), meaning products are favoured.
2. When \(\Delta_r G^\ominus > 0\), \(-RT\ln K > 0 \implies \ln K < 0 \implies K < 1\), meaning reactants are favoured.
3. When \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = 0\), \(\ln K = 0 \implies K = 1\).
4. When \(\Delta_r G = 0\), the free energy of the system is at its minimum and the system is in dynamic chemical equilibrium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\Delta_r G^\ominus < 0\) matches \(K > 1\); \(\Delta_r G^\ominus > 0\) matches \(K < 1\); \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = 0\) matches \(K = 1\); and \(\Delta_r G = 0\) matches a system at dynamic equilibrium.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q15 - Bond dissociation and mean bond enthalpies

questiontext.text:
Match each bond dissociation or atomisation process with its standard enthalpy value at \(298\text{ K}\):

Column IColumn II
1. \(\mathrm{H_2(g) \rightarrow 2H(g)}\)P. \(1665\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
2. \(\mathrm{Cl_2(g) \rightarrow 2Cl(g)}\)Q. \(416\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
3. \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)}\)R. \(435.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
4. Mean \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond enthalpy in \(\mathrm{CH_4(g)}\)S. \(242\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For diatomic molecules, the enthalpy of atomisation equals the bond dissociation enthalpy. For polyatomic molecules like \(\mathrm{CH_4}\), the mean bond enthalpy is the enthalpy of atomisation divided by the number of identical bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
From standard bond enthalpy data at \(298\text{ K}\):
- \(\mathrm{H_2(g) \rightarrow 2H(g)}\) has \(\Delta_{\mathrm{H-H}}H^\ominus = 435.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
- \(\mathrm{Cl_2(g) \rightarrow 2Cl(g)}\) has \(\Delta_{\mathrm{Cl-Cl}}H^\ominus = 242\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
- \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)}\) has \(\Delta_a H^\ominus = 1665\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
- The mean \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond enthalpy in \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) is \(\frac{1}{4}(1665\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) \approx 416\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{H_2(g) \rightarrow 2H(g)}\) matches \(435.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); \(\mathrm{Cl_2(g) \rightarrow 2Cl(g)}\) matches \(242\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)}\) matches \(1665\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); and the mean \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond enthalpy in \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) matches \(416\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MATCH_Q16 - Numerical calculations of entropy Gibbs energy and equilibrium

questiontext.text:
Match each thermodynamic problem with its calculated result (\(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)):

Column IColumn II
1. \(\Delta G^\ominus\) for a reaction with \(K = 10\) at \(300\text{ K}\)P. \(2.4 \times 10^2\)
2. \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}}\) when \(1.00\text{ mol}\) \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) forms at \(298\text{ K}\) (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus = -286\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\))Q. \(T > 2000\text{ K}\)
3. Temperature for spontaneity of \(2\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}\) (\(\Delta H = 400\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\Delta S = 0.2\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\))R. \(-5.744\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
4. Equilibrium constant \(K\) at \(298\text{ K}\) when \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = -13.6\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)S. \(+959.7\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four quantitative problems involving equilibrium constant \(K\), temperature \(T\), \(\Delta G^\ominus\), \(\Delta H^\ominus\), and \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}}\) with \(R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard conditions apply for \(\Delta G^\ominus\) and \(\Delta_f H^\ominus\). For spontaneity at constant \(T\) and \(p\), \(\Delta G < 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. \(\Delta G^\ominus = -2.303 RT \log K\)
2. \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}} = -\frac{\Delta_r H^\ominus}{T}\)
3. \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(\Delta G^\ominus = -2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \log 10 = -5744.1\text{ J mol}^{-1} = -5.744\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
2. \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}} = -\frac{-286 \times 10^3\text{ J mol}^{-1}}{298\text{ K}} = +959.7\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
3. At equilibrium, \(T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S} = \frac{400\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}{0.2\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}} = 2000\text{ K}\). Since \(\Delta H > 0\) and \(\Delta S > 0\), the reaction is spontaneous for \(T > 2000\text{ K}\).
4. \(\log K = \frac{-(-13.6 \times 10^3)}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298} = 2.38 \implies K = \text{antilog}(2.38) = 2.4 \times 10^2\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four calculations match their physical signs and magnitudes: \(K = 10\) at \(300\text{ K}\) gives \(-5.744\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); water formation gives \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}} = +959.7\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\); spontaneity occurs above \(2000\text{ K}\); and \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = -13.6\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) gives \(K = 2.4 \times 10^2\).
